title: Voicing from the top lead down
summary: Smith explains building chords from the trumpet lead, second part a fifth below and baritone on the tonic.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What's the secret of voicing like that? Give it to me in harmonic terms? You'd give the lead to...
To the trumpet.
To the trumpet. Then how would you build the chord on up from there?
Well, you always build....
Especially when you've got five pieces.
Yeah, you build and come down. Build from the leads up top.
So you wouldn't start at the bass.
No.
You would start with the melody lead at the top.
Yeah, way up top.
Then what would be the next thing you'd do? Would you do
Buster Smith - 145
that bottom part or the second part?
No. You'd write the second part, let that be on a fifth...
But the second part on the fifth.
Yeah. He'd be on the fifth.
What happens if the melody happened to be on the fifth?
You just spread them out. If he'd be on the fifth, put him on the tonic.
On the root.
Yeah.
So in other words, you like the lead and the second part a fifth apart.
Yeah.
And then what?
Then if you got a baritone in, you put it way down on the tonic. You got to put it way down.
Would you ever double the bass and the lead?
Mmm-hmm.
Would you ever have it that the lead and the baritone were playing in unison?
Yeah.
You could do that.
Oh yeah, sure. You could do that. Especially when you got too many horns there and you ain't got nowhere else
Buster Smith - 146
to put them. You can't build them chords too deep. That will make it sound out of key.
